name: Insufficient Entropy
principle: The product generates security-sensitive random values with too little entropy, so some outputs are more likely than others. Predictable keys, IVs, salts, tokens, or session IDs can be guessed and used to bypass protection mechanisms.
detection_signals: C/C++ rand(), random(), std::rand(), or std::mt19937 used to generate key, token, session ID, salt, IV, nonce, password, or reset code
Java java.util.Random, Math.random(), or SplittableRandom used to generate key, token, session ID, salt, IV, nonce, password, or reset code
Predictable seeding pattern: srand(time(NULL)), srand(getpid()), srand(userId), Random.setSeed(System.currentTimeMillis()), Random.setSeed(new Date().getTime())
Hard-coded security random value: static final byte[] IV, constant salt, fixed nonce, fixed token secret, or embedded key literal
Small output space for security token: nextInt(n), rand() % n, 6-digit OTP, or token length below 128 bits
Same salt, IV, nonce, or seed reused across users, records, encryptions, processes, or restarts
PRNG output truncated or masked so fixed bits or low-precision values dominate the security value
negative_signals: C/C++ getrandom(), arc4random_buf(), /dev/urandom, BCryptGenRandom(), RAND_bytes(), or libsodium randombytes_buf() used for security value
Java java.security.SecureRandom.nextBytes() used for security value without fixed or predictable setSeed()
Token/key material generated as at least 128 random bits from a CSPRNG before encoding
Per-record password salt generated by bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2, or SecureRandom and stored with the hash
IV/nonce generated uniquely per encryption according to the cipher mode requirements, not hard-coded
Weak PRNG use is limited to non-security code such as shuffling UI items, simulation, tests, or sampling
false_defense_traps: Calling srand(time(NULL)) or Random.setSeed(currentTimeMillis) before generating a token
Hashing a predictable value such as userId, timestamp, or PID and treating the digest as random
Using UUID.randomUUID() where project policy requires explicit CSPRNG token bytes and length checks
Encoding with Base64, hex, or URL encoding and treating the encoded string as added entropy
Using a large-looking decimal range such as nextInt(400000000) for an online-guessable secret
verification_focus: Is every security-sensitive random value generated from enough unpredictable CSPRNG entropy with no predictable seed, fixed value, reuse, or small output space?

consequence_chains.trigger: Predictable token, session ID, API key, or reset code is accepted as authentication proof
consequence_chains.consequence: Attacker guesses the value and authenticates as another user

consequence_chains.trigger: Seed is user ID, timestamp, PID, or another small/predictable space
consequence_chains.consequence: PRNG output has reduced entropy and can be replayed or brute-forced

consequence_chains.trigger: Random-number generation loses precision or reliably emits fixed bits
consequence_chains.consequence: Effective key or token search space is reduced

patch_principle: Use an OS-backed CSPRNG for all keys, tokens, session IDs, salts, IVs, nonces, passwords, and reset codes.
Do not manually seed a CSPRNG with predictable values; never use user IDs, timestamps, PIDs, or fixed constants as seeds.
Generate enough entropy for the purpose, typically at least 128 bits for bearer tokens and algorithm-required sizes for keys.
Generate salts, IVs, and nonces per record or per encryption as required; never hard-code or globally reuse them.
Replace rand(), std::mt19937, java.util.Random, Math.random(), and modulo-reduced PRNG output in security paths.

minimal_examples.safe: byte[] b = new byte[16]; new java.security.SecureRandom().nextBytes(b); String token = Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString(b);
